Evilmerodach
EE-vil-MER-oh-dak
proper n. (king of Babylon who released Jehoiachin)
Hebrew 'evil merodakh, from the Akkadian Amel-Marduk, man of Marduk. The English look of the first syllable is accidental and has nothing to do with evil.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The book of Kings closes not with the fall of Jerusalem but with a small mercy in Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar's son came to the throne in 562 BC, and in his first year he showed kindness to the captive king of Judah. Jeremiah's book ends the same way: “that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the first year of his reign lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison” (Jeremiah 52:31). He “spake kindly unto him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon” (Jeremiah 52:32), and Jehoiachin “did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life” (Jeremiah 52:33). After thirty-seven years in prison, David's heir sat at a king's table. It was a thread, not a restoration; but the thread was the line of David, and God had sworn to keep it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Evilmerodach; the name is that of a king of Babylon, carried into the Authorized Version from the original.

expand to see more

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Evilmerodach.

The name renders the Akkadian Amel-Marduk, man of Marduk.

He was the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar.

He released Jehoiachin from prison in the first year of his reign.

The account closes both 2 Kings and Jeremiah.

Key Scripture

Jer 52:31 — "And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the five and twentieth day of the month, that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the first year of his reign lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison,"

Jer 52:32 — "And spake kindly unto him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon,"

Jer 52:33 — "And changed his prison garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life."

Modern Corruption

The closing note of Kings is treated as an afterthought, when it is the historian's signal that the Davidic promise survived the exile.

expand to see more

Some commentary reads the release of Jehoiachin as a mere archival notice tacked onto a story of total failure. Placed at the very end of Kings and of Jeremiah, it is a deliberate word of hope. Ration tablets from Babylon list Jehoiachin, king of Judah, among those receiving provisions, a striking corroboration of the account.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God to David's house. Jehoiachin's line runs on through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel into the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'evil merodakh from Akkadian Amel-Marduk, man of Marduk; son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar.

expand to see more

Akkadian amel, man, and Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.

2 Kings 25:27 records the release of Jehoiachin.

Jeremiah 52:31 repeats it as the close of Jeremiah's book.

Jeremiah 52:33 gives Jehoiachin a place at the king's table for life.

Matthew 1:12 continues the line of Jechonias toward Christ.

Usage

"Evilmerodach king of Babylon"

"the captive king lifted from prison"

"the thread of David's line in exile"
